nature-eco-696.title: Chemosynthesis: living on chemical energy
nature-eco-696.text:
Deep vents show that life does not need sunlight. Chemosynthesis is the biological conversion of carbon-containing molecules and nutrients into organic matter using energy from oxidising inorganic compounds. Chemoautotrophs obtain carbon from carbon dioxide and are phylogenetically diverse. In most oceanic settings the energy comes from oxidising substances such as hydrogen sulfide or ammonia, with or without oxygen. It supports large animal populations at hydrothermal vents, methane clathrates, cold seeps, whale falls and cave water. Giant tube worms, for example, use bacteria in their trophosome to fix carbon dioxide with hydrogen sulfide as energy.

In 1890 Winogradsky proposed that microbes can live on inorganic matter alone. Hydrothermal vents were found in the 1970s, and the 1977 Galapagos Rift discovery confirmed his idea. Chemosynthesis may even have been the first metabolism to evolve on Earth, before {{ref:nature-eco-212}} and {{ref:nature-eco-190}}.

nature-eco-735.title: Ocean deoxygenation: the sea is losing its breath
nature-eco-735.text:
The oceans have lost 1-2% of their oxygen since the mid-20th century. Ocean deoxygenation is the human-caused reduction of oxygen in parts of the ocean. It occurs in two settings: coastal zones, where eutrophication drives oxygen to very low levels, creating dead zones, and the open and deep ocean, where oxygen minimum zones are expanding.

On the coast, nutrients from urban and agricultural runoff, worsened by deforestation, fuel productivity. The sinking organic matter is respired, using up oxygen and causing hypoxia or anoxia. Warmer water holds less oxygen, so ocean warming adds to the loss and compounds coastal eutrophication. Open ocean areas with no oxygen have grown by more than 1.7 million square miles in 50 years, and coastal low-oxygen areas have grown tenfold. Since 1950 more than 500 coastal sites have reported oxygen below 2 mg per litre, the usual hypoxia threshold. Models predict up to 7% decline in global ocean oxygen over the next hundred years. Less oxygen affects productivity, nutrient and carbon cycling and habitat function, threatening marine life and the people who depend on it for food or livelihood.

nature-eco-729.title: Methanogenesis: how microbes make methane
nature-eco-729.text:
Where oxygen is absent, one group of microbes finishes the job of decay and exhales methane. Methanogenesis is the formation of methane coupled to energy conservation by microbes called methanogens. It is the final stage of anaerobic digestion and the final step in decomposing biomass in anoxic environments. Methanogens come only from the domain Archaea. They respire anaerobically, oxygen inhibits them, and carbon is the terminal electron acceptor. The two best-known pathways use acetic acid or carbon dioxide. Without methanogenesis, a great deal of carbon as fermentation products would accumulate in anaerobic environments.

Flooded soils such as rice fields and wetlands are natural methane sources, though aerating them raises sulfates and nitrates that reduce methane production. Methanogenesis is also the main pathway breaking down landfilled organic matter, and the methane can be collected as biogas fuel.

nature-eco-740.title: Unintended consequences: when actions backfire or surprise
nature-eco-740.text:
Actions in complex systems rarely land only where aimed. Unintended consequences are outcomes of a purposeful action that were neither intended nor foreseen. They fall into three types: unexpected benefits, unexpected drawbacks, and perverse results contrary to the intent. Irrigation schemes can supply farm water yet raise the prevalence of waterborne diseases such as schistosomiasis. Cold War no-man's lands became large natural habitats, an unexpected benefit. Adam Smith's invisible hand is another example, in which agents acting in self-interest contribute to overall economic efficiency.

Robert K. Merton popularised the term. His 1936 causes include ignorance, errors in analysis and immediate interests overriding long-term ones. Causes also include complexity, perverse incentives and cognitive biases. The law of unintended consequences warns that intervening in a complex system tends to produce unanticipated, often undesirable outcomes.

nature-eco-692.title: Bioindicators: species that report on pollution
nature-eco-692.text: A species can act as a gauge of the environment. A bioindicator is a species or group of species whose function, population or status reveals the quality of the environment. Bioindicators show the cumulative effect of pollutants and how long a problem has existed, which physical and chemical testing cannot. A biomonitor is an organism that gives quantitative information on environmental quality, indicating a pollutant and the amount and intensity of exposure. In use, researchers compare an indicator species in a study region with a little-disturbed reference site over time to infer the region's relative environmental health. There is a caution: bioindicators have been reported as inaccurate when applied to geographically and environmentally diverse regions.

nature-eco-734.title: Methanotrophs: microbes that eat methane
nature-eco-734.text:
Some microbes live on the gas that warms the planet. Methanotrophs are prokaryotes that metabolize {{ref:nature-eco-727}} as their source of carbon and chemical energy. They are bacteria or archaea that can grow aerobically or anaerobically, and are common where methane is produced, such as wetlands, soils, rice paddies, landfills and aquatic systems. They matter for global warming because they reduce the amount of methane emitted to the atmosphere in the global methane budget.

Aerobic methanotrophs include Type I and X (Gammaproteobacteria, RuMP pathway) and Type II (Alphaproteobacteria, serine pathway). No aerobic methanotrophic archaea are known. Anaerobic oxidation of methane in marine sediments is mainly done by consortia of methane-oxidizing archaea and sulfate-reducing bacteria. They also have uses. In wastewater plants, methanotroph mixes could cut costs, raise nitrogen removal and produce useful biomolecules, and Methylococcus capsulatus makes animal feed from natural gas.

nature-eco-721.title: Limnology: the science of lakes and rivers
nature-eco-721.text: Limnology is the study of inland aquatic ecosystems. It covers the biological, chemical, physical and geological characteristics of fresh and saline waters: lakes, reservoirs, ponds, rivers, springs, streams, wetlands and groundwater. Water systems are categorized as running (lotic) or standing (lentic). Global limnology considers the role of inland waters in global biogeochemical cycles. François-Alphonse Forel coined the term and founded the field through studies of Lake Geneva.

nature-eco-743.title: Woody plant encroachment: when shrubs take over grassland
nature-eco-743.text:
Open grassland can quietly turn into scrub. Woody plant encroachment is the spread and thickening of native shrubs and bushes at the expense of grasses and forbs. It concerns native plants, not alien invasives, and can shift open grasslands and savannas to closed woodlands. It affects an estimated 500 million hectares on all continents, and the UNCCD names it a key contributor to rangeland loss.

Causes include overgrazing, suppressed wildfires, fewer wild herbivores, land abandonment, and possibly climate change. Once established, shrubs suppress grass. The result is a form of land degradation harming biodiversity, groundwater recharge, carbon storage and herbivore carrying capacity. The cost is economic too: in the western United States, rangeland tree expansion has cost producers an estimated $5 billion since 1990. Encroached grasslands can be a stable state that does not return on its own, and restoring them is difficult.

nature-eco-688.title: Benthos: the community on the bottom
nature-eco-688.text: Benthos is the community of organisms living on, in or near the bottom of a stream, river, lake or ocean. Scientists split it by size into macrobenthos (over about 1 mm), meiobenthos (about 0.1-1 mm) and microbenthos (under about 0.1 mm). By location, endobenthos burrow in the sediment, epibenthos live on top of it and hyperbenthos live just above it. Organic matter reaching the seafloor is consumed or buried, a process called the biological pump, and macrobenthos affect carbon cycling through bioturbation. Because benthic macro-invertebrates are sensitive to contamination that settles in sediments, their number and diversity indicate pollution levels.

nature-eco-679.title: Land reclamation: making new land from water
nature-eco-679.text: Land reclamation is the process of creating new land from oceans, seas, riverbeds or lake beds. Methods include infilling with rock and soil, draining submerged wetlands for farming, and deep cement mixing where dredged material may be contaminated. Draining wetlands is habitat destruction: a 2022 analysis attributed 39% of tidal wetland losses between 1999 and 2019 to direct human action, and nearly 65% of Yellow Sea tidal flats are estimated to have been reclaimed. Reclaimed land is prone to soil liquefaction in earthquakes and to subsidence, and drained marshes sink below surrounding water levels, raising flood danger. Some places now restrict reclamation by law.

nature-eco-728.title: Thermogenic and biogenic methane: two origins
nature-eco-728.text: Methane has two main origins. Thermogenic methane comes from the breakup of organic matter at high temperature and pressure in deep sedimentary strata, and is the most important source of natural gas. Most of Earth's methane, however, is biogenic, made by {{ref:nature-eco-729}} in archaea found in landfills, soils, ruminants, termite guts and anoxic sediments. Methane can also arise by industrial routes.

nature-eco-732.title: Wetland methane feedback: warming wetlands add methane
nature-eco-732.text: Wetlands are the largest natural source of atmospheric methane, about 20-30% of the total. Climate change raises their methane release through higher temperatures and altered rainfall, a phenomenon called wetland methane feedback. More methane, a potent {{ref:nature-eco-162}}, then adds to the warming that drove the release.

nature-eco-684.title: Sediment and coral reef stress
nature-eco-684.text: Coastal development in a watershed is a primary cause of sediment-related stress on coral reefs. Stripping natural vegetation for development exposes soil to wind and rain, so more {{ref:nature-eco-682}} reaches the coast. There it can smother corals, abrade their surfaces and force them to spend energy clearing it.

nature-eco-683.title: Sediment transport: how flows move grains
nature-eco-683.text: Sediment transport is the movement of sediment by flowing water, wind or ice, set by the strength of the flow and the particle's size, volume, density and shape. Stronger flows raise lift and drag on a particle, while larger or denser particles tend to fall out of the flow. Water can move larger sediment than air because it is denser and more viscous. Typical rivers carry sand and gravel, and large floods carry cobbles and boulders. The Exner equation balances sediment in transport against deposition on the bed. Dams make a river pool and deposit its whole load, while dam removal or a fall in base level causes erosion.

nature-eco-719.title: Hydrological models: simplified pictures of the water cycle
nature-eco-719.text: Hydrological models are simplified conceptual representations of part of the hydrologic cycle, used for prediction and for understanding processes. Black box models use mathematical and statistical concepts to link an input such as rainfall to an output such as runoff. Predicting flow and water quality in ungauged basins, where little data exist, is a major current research concern.

nature-eco-720.title: Remote sensing in hydrology: watching water from above
nature-eco-720.text: Remote sensing gives information on hydrologic processes where in situ sensors are sparse, and over large spatial extents. It can measure surface water storage, soil moisture, precipitation, evapotranspiration, and snow and ice. Sources include land-based, airborne and satellite sensors using microwave, thermal and near-infrared data or lidar.

nature-eco-718.title: Statistical hydrology: estimating rare floods and droughts
nature-eco-718.text: Statistical hydrology provides statistical methods to analyse and model parts of the hydrological cycle. Analysing rainfall or river-flow records lets hydrologists estimate future hydrologic phenomena. How often rare events occur is assessed through the return period of such events.
